title: Fix a Workflow That Deploys Untested Pull Requests
intro: A teammate added a deploy job to the CI workflow. It works — too well. It deploys to production on every pull request, including ones whose tests failed.

steps.starter_content:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./deploy.sh
steps.prompt: Fix the 'deploy' job so that it: (1) only runs after 'test' succeeds (needs: test), (2) only runs for pushes to main (e.g. if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'), and (3) runs in the 'production' environment (environment: production), so it gets approval gates and production-scoped secrets.
steps.hint: Jobs in GitHub Actions run in PARALLEL by default — without 'needs', deploy doesn't even wait for test to finish. All three keys (needs, if, environment) go directly under jobs.deploy, at the same level as runs-on.
steps.solution:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./deploy.sh
steps.fake_output:
PR #62: ✓ test   – deploy skipped (not main)
push to main: ✓ test → ⏳ deploy waiting for approval (production)
steps.explanation: Pull requests now only run tests; deploys happen only from main, only after tests pass, and only after the production environment's approval rule.
steps.why: Three independent safety layers, each covering a different failure: 'needs' stops a deploy after failed tests, 'if' stops deploys from branches that were never reviewed, and 'environment' adds a human approval plus keeps production secrets away from PR code entirely. Missing any one of them is a real, common way broken or malicious code reaches production.
